rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: Cryptosporidium is a parasite that causes cryptosporidiosis in people and some animals.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: Transmission can involve infected faeces, farm-animal contact, contaminated recreational or drinking water, raw milk and contaminated produce.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: Cryptosporidiosis is especially common in young children and may be more serious or prolonged in people with weakened immune systems.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: Symptoms commonly include profuse watery diarrhoea, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, low-grade fever and loss of appetite.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: Handwashing with soap and warm water is a core control after toileting, nappy changing and contact with animals.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: People should not swim while symptomatic and for 2 weeks after diarrhoea has stopped.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: People should remain away from work or school until they have been free from diarrhoea and vomiting for at least 48 hours.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: UKHSA publishes laboratory surveillance by year, region, age, sex, season and outbreak context to identify trends.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: Cryptosporidiosis risk depends on parasite species, water treatment, animal or person contact, hygiene, immunity, exposure route and timing.

rows.source: UKHSA cryptosporidiosis prevention and surveillance
rows.verified: UKHSA Cryptosporidium evidence is organism-, water-, animal-, person-, outbreak- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: STEC infection can cause diarrhoea, stomach cramps and fever, and around half of cases may have bloody diarrhoea.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: A small proportion of patients, particularly children, can develop haemolytic uraemic syndrome with kidney-failure risk.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: Cattle are an important STEC O157 reservoir, although other animals can also carry STEC in their faeces.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: Transmission can occur through contaminated food, unpasteurised dairy, animal contact, person-to-person spread and contaminated water.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: STEC has a low infectious dose, making rigorous food, hand and environmental hygiene important.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: Minced meat should be cooked thoroughly and raw food should be separated from cooked or ready-to-eat food.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: There is no specific treatment for uncomplicated STEC; fluids are important and antibiotics are not recommended because they may increase complication risk.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: Suspected HUS requires prompt specimen testing, clinical discussion and notification to the local health-protection team.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: STEC risk depends on strain, food or water source, animal contact, infectious dose, hygiene, host factors and response timing.

rows.source: UKHSA Shiga toxin-producing E. coli management
rows.verified: UKHSA STEC evidence is strain-, food-, animal-, water-, person-, outbreak- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
